title: Measurements for understanding the pace of AI development inside frontier labs
gist: Anthropic publishes first-of-their-kind internal metrics on how fast AI is building AI: as of August 2026 Claude 'leads' 26% of Anthropic's own AI R&D work with over 90% at or above 'AI collaborates', roughly 30,000 internal agents run at any one time with 100% monitor coverage and a 0.002% block rate, and only ~6% of AI R&D compute (12% of AI-driven AI R&D compute) went to safety in a sampled July week. The piece frames these as auditable, cross-lab-comparable indicators that could become triggers for pacing rules and third-party verification.

themes.theme: R&D Automation Index: how much AI builds AI

insights.claim: As of August 2026, Claude autonomously 'leads' 26% of Anthropic's internal AI research and development work, meaning it completes most of the task end-to-end from a high-level prompt while a human only supervises.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A publicly stated, repeatable number for AI-doing-AI-R&D is the closest thing to a leading indicator of recursive self-improvement; track its slope across quarters, not its level.
insights.quote: Claude “leads” 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D work.
insights.locator: As of August 2026,

insights.claim: More than 90% of Anthropic's AI R&D work is already at or above the 'AI collaborates' level, where AI does large chunks of work under close human direction.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Human-only AI research is effectively extinct at a frontier lab; headcount is no longer a clean proxy for research throughput at these firms.
insights.quote: The share of work at or above “AI collaborates” is above 90%.
insights.locator: As of August 2026,

insights.claim: Anthropic states that Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of its AI R&D work, i.e. no task category has reached the top automation level.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The first task category to cross into full autonomy would be the single most newsworthy threshold event in this dataset; watch for it in future releases.
insights.quote: Claude is not operating fully autonomously for any measured subset of AI R&D work.
insights.locator: As of August 2026,

insights.claim: The automation rating uses a six-level 'Automation Level' scale developed by Epoch AI, running from AL0 (no AI involvement) through AL3 'collaborates' and AL4 'leads' to AL5 (fully autonomous, no human in the loop).
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: An externally authored scale is the raw material for cross-lab benchmarking; if other labs adopt AL ratings, automation share becomes a comparable industry metric.
insights.locator: we use an automation rating scale developed by Epoch AI

insights.claim: The index was built bottom-up by randomly sampling 20% of staff per department each week of July 2026 and having a Claude research agent reconstruct their tasks from Slack and internal documentation, yielding roughly 15,000 granular model R&D tasks.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The measurement itself depends on AI agents reading employee work logs, so the audit trail for AI progress is now AI-generated - a structural dependency third parties must be able to re-run.
insights.locator: For each week in July 2026, we randomly sampled 20% of staff

insights.claim: Anthropic organized its R&D tasks into a frozen hierarchical tree of 542 nodes, 378 of them leaves with names like 'eval platform defect diagnosis and fixes', 'RL sandbox egress and network policy' and 'serving incident postmortems'.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Freezing the basket makes the index comparable over time like a CPI basket, which means the published number is an index, not a census, and can drift from reality as work changes.
insights.locator: The resulting tree has 542 nodes at different depths

insights.claim: Rather than judging which research areas matter most, Anthropic weights each task category by person-time, giving each sampled employee one unit of weight per week split evenly across the tasks they worked on.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Person-time weighting will mechanically understate automation exactly where AI has already removed humans from a task, biasing the index downward as automation deepens.
insights.locator: we used the amount of person-time dedicated to that task as a proxy

insights.claim: In validation, the Claude judge model agreed exactly with human raters 59% of the time while humans agreed with each other only 35% of the time, and model and human ratings were within one automation level 97% of the time.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The model is a more consistent rater than the domain experts who own the work - a concrete data point that AI judges can already outperform human inter-rater reliability in fuzzy classification tasks.
insights.quote: model-versus-human exact agreement was 59%, human-versus-human was 35%
insights.locator: Our judge model agreed with humans about as often as humans agreed with each other

insights.claim: Testing whether automation just pushes humans onto new work, Anthropic compared monthly new tasks from February to July 2026 against a January 2026 task basket and found no rise in 'novel' tasks, suggesting the structure of model R&D work is stable at that level of analysis.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: If new human work categories are not appearing inside the lab that builds the models, the 'AI creates new jobs' consolation argument gets weaker evidence at the frontier first.
insights.quote: We found no rise in the number of “novel” tasks between the January and July baskets of tasks
insights.locator: Second, the basket is frozen.

insights.claim: The difference between AL4 and AL5 in Anthropic's worked example is deployment authority: at 'leads' Claude diagnoses, fixes and documents a broken nightly data pipeline but tags an engineer to decide whether it ships, while at 'fully autonomous' it would detect the failure itself and deploy to production unsupervised.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The practical frontier boundary is production deploy rights, not capability - the thing to watch in any lab or enterprise is when the human sign-off gate is removed.
insights.locator: At AL5 (“fully autonomous”)—a level we have not yet reached

themes.theme: Agent fleet scale and monitoring numbers

insights.claim: As of August 2026 roughly 30,000 AI agents were doing research and engineering work at Anthropic at any one time on its most-used internal platform alone.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A concrete headcount-equivalent for internal agent deployment at a frontier lab - a reference point for how far ahead labs are of enterprise agent adoption, and for internal inference demand.
insights.quote: there were approximately 30,000 agents doing research and engineering work at Anthropic at any one time in our most-used internal platform
insights.locator: What we found. As of August 2026

insights.claim: Anthropic analyzed over a billion decisions from its research and engineering agents during August 2026 and found that 0.002% of them, about 1 in 47,000, were blocked by the real-time monitor.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A billion agent decisions in one month at one company quantifies the true unit of AI labor volume, and the 1-in-47,000 block rate is a baseline any future spike would be measured against.
insights.quote: We analyzed over a billion decisions from our research & engineering agents over August 2026 and found that 0.002% of them (about 1 in 47,000) were blocked by this monitor.
insights.locator: Blocking / escalation rate

insights.claim: 100% of the agents' actions pass through an online monitor before execution, usually within seconds, and 100% are also ingested by an offline monitor after the fact.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Full-coverage pre-execution screening is being set up as the implicit industry standard; any lab reporting less than 100% coverage becomes the visible outlier.
insights.locator: Coverage

insights.claim: The offline monitor flags roughly 100,000 agent transcripts per week, about one to two in every thousand, of which only about 50 per week are escalated to human review after classifier triage.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The 100,000-to-50 funnel shows human oversight only survives at agent scale because classifiers do the triage - oversight capacity is itself an AI-dependent bottleneck.
insights.quote: The monitor flags roughly 100,000 transcripts per week
insights.locator: Review latency

insights.claim: Anthropic argues that individually rare agent misbehavior becomes a routine occurrence once millions or billions of agents operate in the economy.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Frames AI incident risk as a volume problem rather than a model-quality problem, which points demand toward monitoring, classifier and audit infrastructure regardless of model reliability gains.
insights.quote: But when there are millions or billions of agents operating in the economy, even rare events can happen regularly.
insights.locator: In our monitoring data to date, individual agents rarely misbehave.

insights.claim: Monitors are split by whether harm is reversible: online monitors block fast irreversible actions such as an agent copying model weights out of company systems, while offline monitors catch slow, reversible problems like signs of model misalignment.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Reversibility-based triage is a transferable control design for any enterprise deploying agents, and defines where latency budgets can and cannot be relaxed.
insights.locator: Online monitors check the actions of agents in real-time

insights.claim: Anthropic proposes coverage, review latency and escalation rate as three standardized, publishable oversight metrics that any developer running agents on its own engineering workloads could report today.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: These three metrics are the likely template for future disclosure regimes; vendors selling agent observability should expect them to become procurement and regulatory line items.
insights.locator: What an AI developer could report today. Any developer running agents

insights.claim: METR has independently red-teamed Anthropic's offline monitoring platform, and Anthropic says developers should disclose how often known agent misbehavior is actually caught by their monitors.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Detection-rate disclosure, not just coverage, is the harder metric - a named external red-teamer is a precedent for a third-party AI assurance market.
insights.locator: In the past, METR has independently red-teamed our offline monitoring platform.

insights.claim: Anthropic gives each internal agent a persistent individual identity that is not tied to a model, so an agent's record stays continuous through model upgrades and every action and data record can be audited back to a specific agent over time.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Model-independent agent identity is an architectural prerequisite for auditing and accountability, hinting at a durable infrastructure layer separate from the model vendor.
insights.quote: because the identity is not tied to a model, it persists through model upgrades, so an agent’s record is continuous even if the underlying model powering it changes
insights.locator: Identity.

insights.claim: Giving agents distinct identities reduces the risk of correlated actions, because an agent can treat another agent's output as a claim to check rather than as its own thought.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Correlated failure across a fleet of identical models is the systemic-risk analogue of everyone holding the same trade; identity separation is the proposed diversification.
insights.quote: treat what comes from another agent as a claim to check rather than a thought of its own
insights.locator: Identity.

insights.claim: Anthropic's agents communicate through a shared open messaging system rather than privately, which prevents 'playing telephone', lets agents correct each other's errors, and allows behavioral monitoring to traverse communications between agents.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Open-by-default inter-agent messaging is a design choice that trades some efficiency for auditability - a likely future compliance expectation for multi-agent systems.
insights.locator: Open communication.

insights.claim: Anthropic concedes it cannot be certain it has a complete picture of agent behaviors at this scale and notes it has been doing this monitoring for months, not years, expecting the science of agent monitoring to change considerably.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The lab with the most agent-monitoring data says the discipline is immature, which means current oversight claims across the industry carry large unmodeled error bars.
insights.quote: We have been doing this kind of monitoring for months, not years, and expect the science of agent monitoring to change considerably going forward.
insights.locator: What this does and doesn’t capture. At this scale of agent activity

themes.theme: Compute allocation and the safety share

insights.claim: In the sampled week of July 13 to July 20, about 6% of the compute that went to AI R&D at Anthropic was allocated toward safety, and about 12% of compute going to AI-driven AI R&D was safety-allocated.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The first published safety-compute share from a frontier lab sets the reference point that rivals and regulators will be measured against, and any commitment to a floor would reprice compute demand.
insights.quote: about 6% of compute that went to AI R&D was allocated toward safety, and about 12% of compute that went to AI-driven AI R&D was allocated toward safety
insights.locator: What we found. Over the examined week,

insights.claim: The safety share is deliberately conservative: any token that advanced capabilities as much as safety was excluded from the safety count, and safeguards classifiers, described as a separate and comparable amount of compute, are not counted at all.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Headline safety-compute percentages are highly sensitive to definitional choices, so cross-lab comparisons without a shared standard will be near-meaningless.
insights.quote: these metrics do not account for safeguards classifiers, which are a separate, comparable amount of compute
insights.locator: These are deliberately conservative estimates.

insights.claim: Compute is a weak proxy for safety effort because safety research is bottlenecked on researchers designing experiments, which is time-consuming, while running those experiments is not particularly compute-intensive.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Any policy that mandates a safety compute quota would be targeting the wrong input; the binding constraint is researcher time, not accelerators.
insights.locator: Safety research tends to use less compute than frontier training runs

insights.claim: Efficiency improvements perversely reduce the measured safety share: a more efficient safety classifier or faster production inference stack changes the ratio without any change in how much safety work is actually done, and Anthropic's own classifier overheads have fallen with efficiency gains.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A falling safety-compute percentage could be a sign of engineering progress rather than deprioritized safety - a trap for anyone trading headlines off this metric.
insights.quote: A more efficient safety classifier, or a faster inference stack for production models, lowers the safety portion, but doesn’t mean we’re doing less safety work.
insights.locator: Third, and most importantly, compute share measures only what is spent.

insights.claim: Anthropic manages compute as a single fungible pool directed dynamically to wherever it is most productive, so the published breakdown is a snapshot of one week's capacity direction rather than a fixed allocation, and the engineering categories do not map to how expenses are classified.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Compute categories in disclosures like this cannot be reconciled to financial statements, so don't try to back out capex or cost structure from safety-share numbers.
insights.quote: We manage compute as a single, fungible pool and direct it dynamically to wherever it is most productive
insights.locator: Footnotes / We manage compute as a single, fungible pool

insights.claim: Rather than classify all of the week's almost 10,000 training and evaluation runs, Anthropic sampled about 14% of them weighted toward the highest-compute runs, so the result reflects where compute actually went rather than run counts.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Nearly 10,000 research runs a week is a usable sizing datapoint for internal experimentation throughput at a frontier lab.
insights.locator: Rather than classify all of the week’s almost 10,000 runs

insights.claim: Anthropic argues compute is among the most verifiable inputs to AI R&D, making it a critical lever for any future effort to coordinate a slowdown in frontier development.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: If pacing rules ever arrive, they will bind on chips and compute accounting rather than on model behavior - relevant to accelerator demand and to chip-tracking policy.
insights.quote: compute is among the most verifiable inputs to the AI R&D process, meaning that it could be a critical lever in a future pacing effort
insights.locator: Why measure compute allocation?

insights.claim: Classifying work as safety versus capabilities is described as difficult but tractable, with a detailed written definition and boundary cases bringing the classifier within one to two percentage points of human reviewers, though some cases stayed undecidable even after several hours of human review.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Shows AI classifiers can already deliver regulator-grade categorization if definitions are written carefully - the bottleneck is the definition, not the classifier.
insights.locator: The main lesson of this exercise is that classifying what is and isn’t safety work is difficult but tractable

insights.claim: Scalable oversight research is offered as the canonical hard boundary case, because it might make future models more aligned and current models more commercially useful at the same time.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Safety and commercial value are not cleanly separable at the research level, which undercuts any regime that tries to ringfence 'safety spending'.
insights.locator: For example, research on scalable oversight

insights.claim: Anthropic identifies two obstacles to cross-lab comparison of automation metrics: the absence of a common methodology, and the fact that a lab uses its own models to evaluate its own systems, so the judge model could make the same kinds of errors as the model it is checking.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Correlated judge-model error is the core credibility gap in all AI self-reporting; the fix - cross-lab model evaluation - requires sharing competitively sensitive data.
insights.quote: we’re using our own models to evaluate our systems, which could mean that the “judge” model could make the same kinds of errors as the model it is checking
insights.locator: Two obstacles stand in the way of cross-lab comparison

insights.claim: Anthropic plans to embed independent third-party evaluators from multiple organizations inside the company with access to internal processes, systems and data comparable to what internal risk assessment teams have, tasked with verifying safety practices, reporting incidents and monitoring these metrics.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Embedded external auditors at a frontier lab would create a new assurance function - watch which organizations get the seats and whether rivals follow.
insights.quote: We plan to embed independent third-party evaluators from multiple organizations at Anthropic
insights.locator: It’s important to note that we would expect these numbers to shift

insights.claim: Anthropic argues the burden of proof should sit with the developer to show that work is safety-related, because each developer will be tempted to draw the safety/capabilities line generously.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: An explicit warning that self-reported safety numbers are gameable, coming from the lab publishing them - treat unaudited rival disclosures accordingly.
insights.quote: The burden of proof should sit with the developer to show that work is safety-related.
insights.locator: Safety research is hard to distinguish from capabilities research

insights.claim: Many of the underlying labels used in the compute measurement - reasons for runs, workload tags, the source of API traffic - are set by automated rules or by users and are best-effort rather than verified, so mislabeled usage would not necessarily be caught.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Today's infrastructure cannot produce audit-grade compute accounting; making these disclosures enforceable implies new instrumentation and telemetry spending.
insights.quote: A measurement meant to be trusted by outsiders will need to be complete, accurate, and technically enforced.
insights.locator: Three further limitations matter.

insights.claim: Anthropic proposes that these measurements could become triggers for stronger requirements, naming a fixed testing window before a new model is used for further AI R&D, commitments on the share of compute going to safety research, and limits on the share of compute going to AI research agents.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: These are the concrete shapes future AI regulation could take, and each would directly throttle internal model-development velocity at every frontier lab.
insights.locator: These measures could also become the trigger for stronger requirements

insights.claim: Anthropic says the compute measurement covers only one week, which is enough to show the measurement can be made but not enough to establish a meaningful trend.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Treat the 6%/12% safety-compute figures as a proof of concept, not a baseline to extrapolate from until repeated disclosures exist.
insights.locator: Second, the measurement covers one week

themes.theme: Pacing the frontier as a policy frame

insights.claim: Anthropic explicitly expects these internal automation and compute numbers to shift if there were industry coordination on pacing the frontier, a slowdown called for by CEO Dario Amodei.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The leading US lab is publicly laying groundwork for a coordinated slowdown regime, which would reshape the competitive race dynamic and compute demand curve if it gains traction.
insights.quote: we would expect these numbers to shift if there were coordination on pacing the frontier, as called for by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei
insights.locator: It’s important to note that we would expect these numbers to shift

insights.claim: Anthropic frames the goal of transparency as minimizing the gap between what frontier labs know and what the public knows, so that society gets a chance to decide how to use the information.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Positions voluntary disclosure as a pre-emptive move ahead of mandated reporting, and as competitive differentiation against less transparent labs.
insights.quote: we should do everything possible to minimize the gap between what frontier labs know and what the public knows
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: These production-process metrics are positioned as complements to capability evaluations, which Anthropic publishes separately through Responsible Scaling Policy risk reports that include evidence on how much its models accelerate AI R&D, while its Advanced AI Framework proposes transparency obligations governments could require.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Two-track disclosure - inputs plus outputs - is the template Anthropic wants written into regulation; RSP risk reports are the other document to monitor.
insights.locator: Reasons to track these measurements

insights.claim: Anthropic argues that AI building AI cuts both ways: it lets labs in democratic countries develop more capable models faster and run more safety testing before release, while models accelerating their own development could make it harder for humans to understand or control them.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: The geopolitical framing - stay on the frontier for democratic countries - is the standing argument against unilateral slowdown, which is why Anthropic pushes for coordinated pacing instead.
insights.locator: Why measure AI-led R&D?

insights.claim: The stated purpose of the automation index is to let outsiders see how close the world is to recursive self-improvement, defined as a model fully autonomously building its successor.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete operational definition of a threshold that until now has been rhetorical, making it measurable and therefore potentially regulable.
insights.quote: recursive self improvement (a model fully autonomously building its successor)
insights.locator: Why measure AI-led R&D?

insights.claim: Anthropic's stated aim in measuring the production process is to correlate model inputs like compute with model outputs like capabilities, giving a better handle on what drives capability gains.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: If input-output correlation becomes publishable, outsiders could forecast capability jumps from observable compute - a potentially tradeable signal.
insights.quote: By better understanding the production process of models, we have a better chance of correlating model inputs, like compute, with model outputs, like capabilities.
insights.locator: Reasons to track these measurements
